ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Martin Luther — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: New patient visit for attacks of vertigo with left-ear tinnitus and muffled hearing, and low mood: history, neurological and ear examination, blood and urine tests, depression and safety screening, and an otology referral

text.paragraph: New patient visit for attacks of vertigo with left-ear tinnitus and muffled hearing, and low mood: history, neurological and ear examination, blood and urine tests, depression and safety screening, and an otology referral [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: He is frightened of another attack, especially while preaching or teaching, and of losing the hearing in his left ear. [S]
He has felt low and abandoned for weeks and wonders whether the attacks are a spiritual trial rather than an illness. [S]
He remembers the pain of the stone last year and wants to avoid another. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Martin Luther was born on 10 November 1483 (Julian calendar) in Eisleben, into a relatively prosperous mining family; his father, Hans, gave him a good education and intended him for law. [D]

He entered the University of Erfurt in 1501 and became a Master of Arts in 1505; later in 1505, after a vow to St Anna made in a thunderstorm, he entered the Augustinian monastery at Erfurt against his father's wishes, and he was ordained in 1507. [D]

As a monk, although he made full use of confession, he felt that he was 'a sinner before God with an extremely disturbed conscience', and this anxiety and fear meant that he underwent what he termed Anfechtungen, spiritual trials or temptations, in particular about predestination. [D]

He became professor of the Bible at Wittenberg in 1512 and held the post until his death. He published the Ninety-Five Theses on 31 October 1517, refused to recant at the Diet of Worms in 1521, was declared an outlaw, was sheltered at the Wartburg, and returned to Wittenberg on 6 March 1522. [D]
In 1525 he married Katharina von Bora, a former nun; they had six children, two daughters of whom died young. [D]
In May 1521, at the Wartburg, he wrote to Philipp Melanchthon that the Lord had afflicted him with painful constipation, and that he had not slept all night. [D]

In the autumn of 1510, in Bologna, he reported severe headache and whizzing in the ear; from 1523, according to his physician Matthias Ratzeberger, he had regular headaches with fainting spells and vertigo. [D]

From 1526 on he had sporadic attacks of urinary stones, which reminded him of death because of the excruciating pain; the first stone, in 1526, was preceded by headache, heaviness in the head, vertigo and nausea and was passed through the urethra. [D]
On 22 April 1527 (Julian) a severe attack of dizziness forced him to break off a sermon. [D]

On the evening of 6 July 1527 (Julian), when he was 43, he had an attack that began with a roaring tinnitus in his left ear, which increased and seemed to fill the left half of his head, followed by nausea, pallor, coldness and a state of collapse without loss of consciousness; he prayed and believed he would not survive the night. After a night's rest all the symptoms had subsided except the tinnitus, which persisted. His friends Justus Jonas and Johannes Bugenhagen wrote accounts of it. [D]
In the first half of 1527 he was deeply disturbed by disputes with other reformers over the Lord's Supper and suffered severe depression. [D]

Feldmann concluded from Luther's letters and his friends' reports that the attacks with tinnitus and vertigo that began in 1527 were a typical case of Ménière disease of the left ear, more than 330 years before Ménière's description; earlier writers had read them as a psychiatric disorder or as chronic inflammation of the middle ear, and a later Japanese review reads them as chronic suppurative otitis media. [R]

Evers, applying modern criteria to the letters, found that some of his vertigo attacks met the criteria for Ménière disease, that others occurred with headaches meeting the criteria for vestibular migraine, and that his headaches partly met the criteria for migraine; he concluded that vestibular migraine with migraine and Ménière disease is possible but not final. [R]

text.paragraph: 7 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

tr.td: Recurrent spiritual crises with anxiety, fear and a deeply troubled conscience since his years as a monk in his twenties, which he called Anfechtungen
Headaches with noises in the ears since his late twenties, and headaches with faint spells and dizziness reported by his physician for about four years
Painful constipation with sleeplessness in his late thirties
A urinary stone passed last year after excruciating pain, preceded by headache, heaviness in the head, dizziness and nausea
Severe low mood earlier this year during bitter disputes in his work

list.item: University professor of biblical studies, preacher and prolific writer; long working days, frequent public controversy, and many letters and visitors [S]
Married for two years, with a young child; a large household that often includes students and guests [S]
Faith is central to his life; he prays daily and describes his low periods in religious terms, as trials [S]
Tobacco: never. Alcohol: beer with the evening meal, about two a day (AUDIT-C 3). No other drugs. Coffee: three to four cups a day [S]
Physical activity: walks in the town; no regular exercise. Diet: hearty, with salted meats, bread and fish; drinks little water [S]

tr.td: Meclizine 25 mg tablet, one by mouth up to every 8 hours during a severe vertigo attack only, for no more than 3 days at a time
every 8 hours as needed during a severe attack, at most 3 days at a time

text.paragraph: Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Well-built man, articulate and forceful; mood low, affect constricted but reactive, warming when he speaks of his work; describes guilt and a sense of being abandoned during the attacks; no suicidal ideation, intent or plan; no psychotic features; insight good. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

text.paragraph: Alert and engaged. Independent; had to stop preaching mid-sermon during one attack and was unable to work for about a week after the worst one; fears an attack in public. [S]

Vital signs recorded on 1527-07-28; see the Vital Signs section. Mental status: Well-built man, articulate and forceful; mood low, affect constricted but reactive, warming when he speaks of his work; describes guilt and a sense of being abandoned during the attacks; no suicidal ideation, intent or plan; no psychotic features; insight good. The physical examination is limited to the findings relevant to this synthetic episode. [S]

Structured safety assessment: current ideation absent, intent absent, plan absent, access to means reviewed: yes. No suicidal ideation, intent, plan or past attempts; during the worst attack he believed he would die but did not wish to. Outpatient care with a safety plan, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and the clinic number, and review at every visit. [S]

list.item: Recurrent attacks of spinning vertigo for about three months, the worst twelve days ago, lasting hours, with roaring tinnitus, fullness and muffled hearing in the left ear and nausea, the tinnitus persisting between attacks; with low mood, poor sleep and loss of interest; cause not established at intake: an inner-ear disorder suspected, with vestibular migraine, vestibular schwannoma and posterior circulation stroke to be excluded and depression to be assessed; otology consultation requested: active, confirmed [S]
Urinary stone disease: one stone passed spontaneously last year after severe pain; stone type and metabolic risk not yet known at intake: active, confirmed [S]
Otology (neurotology) consultation in two weeks, with audiometry, to confirm the cause of the attacks and plan treatment. Guideline: Clinical Practice Guideline: Ménière's Disease (2020) [S]

Diagnostic work-up at intake: ear and neurological examination, positional testing, blood count, kidney function and electrolytes, calcium, uric acid, TSH and urinalysis; a symptom diary of each attack (start, duration, hearing, tinnitus, ear fullness, headache, light sensitivity); formal audiometry at the otology visit. Guideline: Clinical Practice Guideline: Ménière's Disease (2020); Diagnostic criteria for Menière's disease (2015); Vestibular migraine: diagnostic criteria (update) (2022) [S]

Meclizine only for severe attacks, for no more than three days at a time; sit or lie down at the first warning; no driving, ladders or swimming alone while attacks are active. Guideline: Clinical Practice Guideline: Ménière's Disease (2020) [S]

Depression: PHQ-9 at every visit, a structured diagnostic interview at the next visit, and a safety plan with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and the clinic number. Guideline: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Depression Across Three Age Cohorts (2019); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024) [S]

Stone history: drink enough water to pass at least 2.5 liters of urine a day; serum calcium and uric acid at intake; stone analysis and metabolic testing if another stone occurs. Guideline: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline (2014) [S]
Referral to otolaryngology (otology/neurotology), Friedrich Okafor-Lindqvist, MD, ordered 1527-07-28 [S]
